dissented.claim_defeated: the new LOOSE comment describes what the detector does not take (scripts/sov_status_claims.py: It does NOT take the exotic forms - an anchored or tagged key, the explicit-key `? ` form, a leading BOM or zero-width space, or a key containing a space, colon, plus, at, percent or parenthesis)
dissented.finding: The enumeration is my sample, not the class. I reported sixteen shapes; they were written into the comment; the real set is much larger, and I established it by sweeping every printable ASCII character rather than by listing examples. Twenty-nine characters placed inside a key produce a valid YAML mapping with a `_status`-suffixed key that is invisible to BOTH readers, earning neither FIELD_UNTYPED nor FIELD_UNREADABLE: space, exclamation, double quote, hash, dollar, percent, ampersand, apostrophe, both parentheses, asterisk, plus, comma, colon, semicolon, less-than, equals, greater-than, question mark, at, both square brackets, backslash, caret, backtick, both braces, pipe and tilde. The comment names seven of the twenty-nine - space, percent, the two parentheses, plus, colon and at - and leaves twenty-two unnamed, including the quote, comma, semicolon, asterisk, pipe, bracket and brace forms. Fourteen characters do the same in leading position: dollar, both parentheses, plus, dot, slash, colon, semicolon, less-than, equals, question mark, backslash, caret and tilde. And every non-ASCII letter I tried is invisible: a Cyrillic a, a Greek omicron and an accented Latin e each produce a valid YAML key ending in _status that neither reader sees, and none of that category is named at all.
dissented.consequence: Zero behavioural risk, and I want that stated before anything else: no standing is derived, none of these occurs in STATUS.yaml - which carries no BOM, no CRLF and no non-ASCII byte, and whose full YAML parse agrees exactly with the strict reader - and the worst case remains a field going untyped rather than falsely typed. All three of those claims in the comment are true and I verified each. The finding is that the sentence replaced a universal overclaim with an enumeration that reads as complete and is not, which is the same habit in its seventh spelling and the one this concern keeps meeting. It is also the one instance where I am part of the cause: I gave sixteen shapes as evidence of a class and they were transcribed as the class. The rule is already in the file and is shorter than the list - LOOSE requires a leading [A-Za-z0-9] followed by a run of ASCII letters, digits, underscore, dot, hyphen and slash, so any character outside that set anywhere in the key makes the line invisible to both readers. One clause, derived from the pattern rather than sampled from a witness, complete at any character set, and carrying the same virtue the two key-set repairs in this very commit just adopted.
dissented.what_would_have_defeated_this_finding: stating the character class instead of the examples - it does not take a key containing any character outside ASCII letters, digits, underscore, dot, hyphen and slash - which is true of all forty-three characters I found and of every one I did not try; or dropping the second half of the sentence entirely and keeping only the true statements that none occurs in STATUS.yaml and that the worst case is an untyped field.

landing_assessment.my_view: The substance is done. Both key-set claims are now true at any size, the key-count class is closed with no seventh site, behaviour is unmoved and proven so twice over, and the delta is clean. The one finding is a comment that enumerates my sixteen shapes where the real set is twenty-nine ASCII characters inside a key, fourteen leading, and every non-ASCII letter. It carries no behavioural risk and it is one clause to fix, and the clause is already in the file as the LOOSE character class. I would confirm on a reading of a commit that states the character class instead of the examples, or that drops the enumeration and keeps the two true sentences, provided the budget is re-measured on a quiet box.

standing_supported: Supports OPEN to BUILT for the ten paths and supports the claim that R3-B1 is closed. Both key-set statements are now size-agnostic and true, and extending the repair to the corpus case - which I had graded correct - was right, because a claim true only at the current size is the same defect dormant. An exhaustive prose sweep finds no seventh key-count site anywhere in the ten landing paths, and every surviving count checks out against measurement. The change is prose-only, proven by AST equality with the LOOSE pattern byte-identical, and behaviour is unmoved under the full battery re-run rather than inferred. It does not support BUILT to WITNESSED, on one finding inside the part of the repair I did not ask for. The new LOOSE comment replaced a universal overclaim with an enumeration that reads as complete and is not: twenty-nine ASCII characters inside a key make a valid YAML status key invisible to both readers and the comment names seven; fourteen do so in leading position; every non-ASCII letter does and none is named. The three factual claims around it - that these forms are absent from STATUS.yaml, that no standing is derived, that the worst case is an untyped field - are each true and each verified. This is the seventh spelling of the habit this concern keeps meeting, and it is the one I helped cause by offering sixteen shapes as evidence of a class. The rule is already in the file and shorter than the list: any character outside ASCII letters, digits, underscore, dot, hyphen and slash makes the key invisible. Separately and not as a defect in the change, the verification budget failed on both sides tonight including on main, so the verify PASS the grant requires cannot be read from these runs and needs a quiet box.

judgement_items.question: Unchanged: contracts/status-claims.json names decisions/0074 as its governing decision and that record cannot land with the code, because decisions/ is outside grant:standing-landing-loop. Should verify grade a contract's decision and governed_by paths for existence, forcing a contract to land with its decision, or is a contract permitted to name its governing decision before the record exists?

Three readings have now each found prose describing the artifact more confidently than the code supports, and each repair was correct and reachable by the next reader. The durable move in this commit was not fixing a number but writing the claim so no size of the set can falsify it. Is the general rule worth stating somewhere - that a claim about an artifact should be written against the rule that produces it rather than against the examples a witness happened to bring - or has this concern paid enough for that lesson to leave it in the record and stop?
